passage_text: Researchers studied the effects of a novel dietary supplement on glucose metabolism in adult mice. The study employed a randomized controlled design with 60 male C57BL/6 mice divided into three groups: a control group receiving a standard diet, a low-dose supplement group receiving 50 mg/kg/day, and a high-dose supplement group receiving 200 mg/kg/day. Over 12 weeks, researchers measured fasting blood glucose, insulin tolerance, and body weight weekly. At the end of the study, glucose tolerance tests (GTT) were performed, and insulin signaling pathways were examined via Western blot analysis of the Akt pathway in liver tissue. The data suggested that the high-dose group exhibited a significant reduction in fasting blood glucose (mean 120 mg/dL vs 180 mg/dL in controls) and improved insulin sensitivity, while the low-dose group showed intermediate effects. However, the high-dose group also experienced a slight increase in liver weight, raising concerns about potential hepatic side effects. These findings highlight a dose-dependent response but also underscore the importance of monitoring organ-specific toxicity when evaluating new metabolic interventions.
stem: Based on the data presented, which of the following statements best describes the dose-dependent effect of the supplement on glucose metabolism?

options.A: The supplement has no effect on glucose metabolism at any dose.
options.B: Only the low-dose supplement improves glucose metabolism, while the high-dose has no effect.
options.C: Both low- and high-dose supplements improve glucose metabolism, with the high-dose showing a greater effect.
options.D: The high-dose supplement worsens glucose metabolism compared to the control.

explanation: The table shows a progressive decrease in fasting blood glucose and an increase in insulin sensitivity from control to low-dose to high-dose, indicating a dose-dependent improvement in glucose metabolism.
trap: Assuming that the high-dose supplement is always better without considering potential toxicity.

options.C: Use of a male mouse strain.
options.D: Conducting a glucose tolerance test at study end.

explanation: Randomization minimizes confounding variables and ensures that differences in outcomes are attributable to the intervention rather than pre-existing differences among the mice.

stem: Which of the following interpretations of the study is a misreading of the data?

options.A: Because glucose fell dose-dependently, the supplement is shown to have no hepatic effects
options.B: The high-dose group had a lower mean fasting glucose than the control group
options.C: The high-dose group had a higher mean liver weight than the control group
options.D: The high-dose group had the highest insulin sensitivity index of the three groups

explanation: Correct: The table shows liver weight rising from 1.8 g (control) to 2.1 g (high dose), and the passage raises hepatic concerns, so efficacy on glucose does not demonstrate hepatic safety. Why the others are wrong: B) Fasting glucose was 120 versus 180 mg/dL, so this is supported. C) Liver weight was 2.1 versus 1.8 g, so this is supported. D) ISI was 1.9 in the high-dose group versus 1.5 and 1.2, so this is supported.
trap: Assuming that a good efficacy result on glucose also proves the supplement is safe for the liver.
